food.text: Massaman curry, a Thai dish, is a fusion of foreign ingredients from three regions, Persia, the Indian subcontinent and the Malay Archipelago, with ingredients more commonly used in native Thai cuisine. The foreign flavours include cardamom, cinnamon, cloves, star anise, cumin, bay leaves, nutmeg and mace.

In the 17th century, the spices in massaman curry paste would have been brought to Thailand from the Malay Archipelago and South Asia by foreigners. The trade was originally dominated by Muslim traders, but was increasingly undertaken by the Portuguese, the Dutch, and the French East India Company.

In the 16th and 17th centuries, Portuguese, Spanish, Dutch, French and British traders all competed for a monopoly on Southeast Asia's spice trade. Europeans prized spices such as pepper, cinnamon, nutmeg and cloves, and demand for them was high. This trade drove the first phase of European colonisation of the region.

Some New World vegetables, including chili peppers and corn (maize), reached Vietnam by way of the Ming dynasty. Chili peppers would eventually become one of the characteristic flavours of Vietnamese cooking, with bird's eye chili giving its dishes their spicy note.

According to Thai scholars and food experts including Santi Sawetwimon and David Thompson, massaman curry originated in 17th century central Thailand at the cosmopolitan court of Ayutthaya. They say it came through the Persian merchant Sheik Ahmad Qomi, from whom the noble Thai Bunnag family descends.

Portugal became the first European power to establish a bridgehead in maritime Southeast Asia, with its conquest of the Sultanate of Malacca in 1511. The Dutch later took Malacca from the Portuguese in 1641. Control of this key port was part of the struggle over the spice trade.

To secure exclusive access to the centres where pepper, cloves, nutmeg, mace and cinnamon were produced, European nations competed fiercely and violence was commonplace. In the 17th century the Dutch and the Spanish wrestled control of the spice trade from the Portuguese. In the 18th century the British gained control of it from the Dutch.

As European trade routes replaced the old Maritime Silk Route, demand for Southeast Asian spices continued, but the spices were now linked by direct routes to the European market rather than passing through regional Indian Ocean ports. Meanwhile, the jong, the formerly dominant Southeast Asian trading ship, ceased to be built by the 17th century.

From the 18th century onwards, the ingredients and dishes of the Mekong Delta's indigenous Khmer Krom influenced the cuisine of southern Vietnam, as large numbers of Vietnamese settled there. The influence included spices such as cardamom, cinnamon, star anise, clove, ginger, turmeric and ground coriander, along with curries and fermented foods.

The Bunnag family, descended from the Persian-born merchant Sheikh Ahmad, kept funeral cookbooks. These include Massaman curry along with other dishes inspired by Persian dishes, preserving a culinary link to Persia within a Thai noble family.

The 17th-century spices in Massaman curry, including cardamom, cinnamon, cloves, nutmeg and mace, were brought to Thailand from the Malay Archipelago and South Asia. The trade was first dominated by Muslim traders, but was increasingly carried out by the Portuguese, the Dutch and the French East India Company.

Southeast Asia's formerly dominant trading ships, called jong, gave English the word "junk". Their shipbuilding declined until it ceased entirely by the 17th century, as European trade routes replaced the old regional ones.

In the 17th and 18th centuries, European conquests focused on ports along the maritime routes, which gave trade a secure passage. Holding these ports also let foreign rulers levy taxes and control the prices of Southeast Asia's highly desired commodities, spices among them.

Pea shoots are generally believed to have been introduced to Southeast Asia by the Hmong people. Increasing restrictions on Hmong freedoms in the 17th century caused them to migrate out of China into Southeast Asia, carrying with them the habit of cooking the tender tips of the pea plant.

Massaman curry is extolled in the poem Kap He Chom Khrueang Khao Wan from the end of the 18th century. It is attributed to Prince Itsarasunthon of Siam, the later King Rama II (1767 to 1824), and dedicated to a lady thought to be Princess Bunrot, the later Queen Sri Suriyendra.

food.text: Some food experts say Massaman curry began in 17th century Ayutthaya, through the Persian merchant Sheik Ahmad Qomi. Many theories instead say it is a southern Thai dish influenced by Malay and Indian cuisine. A poem from the end of the 18th century, attributed to Prince Itsarasunthon, praises the curry.

art.text: From 1565 to 1815, Filipino craftsfolk built the Manila galleons used for trade from Asia to the Americas. Many of the goods that crossed on these ships went on to Europe.
San Agustin Church in Manila was built in 1607. The building has been declared a World Heritage Site, and it is famous for its painted interior.
By 1600, the Rice Terraces of the Philippine Cordilleras had been made. Five rice terrace clusters have since been designated as World Heritage Sites.
tags: Rice Terraces of the Philippine Cordilleras

art.text: In 1565, the ancient tradition of tattooing in the Philippines was first recorded through the Pintados. Their body art is one of the earliest documented in the islands.
The Ho Phakeo temple was built in the 16th century by King Setthatirath. Today it is a popular museum that houses many famous artworks created in Laos.
The Monreal Stones were created in Ticao, Masbate, following 1621. They are one of the Philippine artworks recorded from the early Spanish era.
In 1680, the Arch of the Centuries was made. In 1692, the image of Nuestra Senora de la Soledad de Porta Vaga was painted.
tags: Nuestra Senora de la Soledad de Porta Vaga

war.text: European powers competing for the valuable spice trade soon sought to eliminate each other by forcibly taking control of production centers, trade hubs and strategic locations. This began with the Portuguese acquisition of Malacca in 1511. Later conquests focused on ports along the maritime routes.

The Trịnh-Nguyễn War lasted from 1627 until 1672. Between 1600 and 1775 the two powerful families partitioned Vietnam, with the Nguyễn lords ruling Đàng Trong in the south and the Trịnh lords controlling Đàng Ngoài in the north.

In 1641 the Dutch took Malacca from the Portuguese. Earlier, in 1619, the Dutch East India Company had taken the city of Sunda Kelapa and renamed it Batavia, now Jakarta, as a base for trading and expansion into the rest of Java.

The Trịnh army staged at least seven offensives in the Trịnh-Nguyễn War, all of which failed to capture Phú Xuân. From 1651 the Nguyễn themselves went on the offensive, but Trịnh Tạc forced them back by 1655.

The civil war between the Lê-Trịnh and Mạc dynasties ended in 1592, when the army of Trịnh Tùng conquered Hanoi and executed king Mạc Mậu Hợp. After this, the Lê monarchs were only figureheads, and real power in the north belonged to the Trịnh lords.
Manila gained two fortifications in quick succession. Fort San Antonio Abad was completed in 1584, and Fort Santiago was built in 1591.

In 1592 the army of Trịnh Tùng conquered Hanoi and executed king Mạc Mậu Hợp, ending the civil war between the Lê-Trịnh and the Mạc. Survivors of the Mạc royal family fled to the northern mountains in Cao Bằng province and continued to rule there. Their last territory was conquered in 1677 by Trịnh Tạc.
During the Vietnamese civil war, the Ming court reluctantly decided on a military intervention. However, Mạc Đăng Dung offered ritual submission to the Ming Empire, and it was accepted.

Britain's East India Company, led by Josiah Child, was effectively expelled from the region following the Siam-England war of 1687. Britain turned its attention to the Bay of Bengal after 1783, having struggled with the French for naval superiority and needing good harbours.

literature.text: Between the 15th and 19th centuries, popular literature and folk songs in Vietnam were written in Vietnamese using a script called chữ Nôm. It was derived from Chinese characters, known as chữ Hán. Meanwhile, Classical Chinese remained the language of formal writing until the 19th century.

Chữ Nôm was regarded as inferior to Chinese, but it gradually grew in prestige. It flourished in the 18th century, when many notable Vietnamese writers and poets composed their works in it. It briefly became the official written script.

During the French colonial period, a Latin script romanizing the Vietnamese language was introduced in Vietnam alongside Catholicism. Called chữ Quốc Ngữ, or 'National Language Script', it is the Vietnamese alphabet in use today.

Between the 15th and 19th centuries, Vietnamese popular literature and folk songs were written in the Vietnamese language using chữ Nôm, a script derived from Chinese characters. Meanwhile, Classical Chinese remained the language of formal writing until the 19th century.

The Vietnamese alphabet was created in the 17th century. It did not become popular outside missionary groups until the early 20th century, when the French colonial administration mandated its use in French Indochina. By the mid-20th century, virtually all Vietnamese literature was composed in it.

The poet Hồ Xuân Hương was born at the end of the 18th century. She composed much of her poetry in chữ Nôm, and most of it has since been translated into the Vietnamese alphabet for modern readers. Her poetry continues to be widely popular.

In the 18th century, Vietnamese scholars competed in poetry-writing contests with Chinese and Korean scholars. Lê Quý Đôn's triumph in such a competition became a focus of national pride. He is considered the last great author of Chinese literature in Vietnam.
Lê Quý Đôn's output was prodigious. It included a history of Vietnam, collected essays on a wide variety of topics, anthologies of verse, and commentaries on the classics.

During the Tây Sơn dynasty (1778–1802), Vietnamese written in Nôm briefly replaced Literary Chinese as the official government language. Nguyễn Huệ attempted similar reforms from 1788. They were reversed at the beginning of the succeeding Nguyễn dynasty.
In 1613, the oldest surviving suyat writing on paper was written. It survives in the University of Santo Tomas Baybayin Documents.

science.text: By the 16th century, Europeans were coming to Đại Việt to trade. The Trịnh and Nguyễn lords bought Western weapons to equip their armies, and muskets began to be imported. Even so, Đại Việt's own firearm techniques were considered highly advanced, from small-caliber matchlock guns to cannons.

The Ming dynasty rated the Đại Việt arquebus as "the best gun in the world". It ranked above the Ottoman gun, the Japanese gun and the European gun. Western observers also praised its high accuracy after seeing it in the Lê-Mạc and Trịnh-Nguyễn wars.

Southeast Asia's formerly dominant trading ships were called jong, the source of the English word "junk". After the colonial era disrupted the Maritime Silk Route, jong shipbuilding declined until it ceased entirely by the 17th century. Chinese-built chuán ships survived until modern times.

The great Southeast Asian trading ships called jong, the source of the English word 'junk', were once dominant. Shipbuilding of them declined until it ceased entirely by the 17th century, while Chinese-built chuán survived until modern times.

In his Suma Oriental of 1515, Tomé Pires wrote that Cochinchina had an innumerable number of musketeers and small bombards. He also noted that a lot of gunpowder was used there, both in warfare and in amusements.

Đại Việt muskets did not stay within Vietnam. They were introduced to China after border conflicts between the Mạc dynasty and ethnic minorities in Guangxi and Yunnan. Firearms were also widely used by civilians in daily life in Đại Việt.
The Đại Việt gun could penetrate several layers of iron armor and kill from 2 to 5 people with a single bullet. It was also said to fire without emitting any loud sounds.

A Qing-era record, the Nányuè bǐjì, linked the Vietnam arquebus with the Java arquebus. This suggests that the firearm known for its accuracy in Đại Việt was connected in people's minds with a similar weapon from the island of Java.

politics.text: Portugal became the first European power to gain a foothold in maritime Southeast Asia when it conquered the Sultanate of Malacca in 1511. The Netherlands and Spain followed and soon superseded Portugal as the main European powers in the region.

European powers competed fiercely for a monopoly over the valuable spice trade, and they sought to eliminate each other by forcibly taking control of production centers, trade hubs and strategic locations. Throughout the 17th and 18th centuries, conquests focused on ports along the maritime routes, which let foreign rulers levy taxes and control prices.

The Mạc dynasty ruled a unified Vietnam from 1527 to 1540, then only northern Vietnam. Its founder Mạc Đăng Dung rose after the Lê emperors Lê Uy Mục and Lê Tương Dực were assassinated, then won a court power struggle that became a civil war. In 1522 he forced Emperor Lê Chiêu Tông to abdicate and installed a puppet, Lê Cung Hoàng. Lê Chiêu Tông fled and fought on until he was defeated and captured in 1526. In 1527 Mạc Đăng Dung removed Lê Cung Hoàng and took the throne himself, and some Confucian officials who rejected the usurpation were killed.

The Maritime Silk Route was replaced by European trade routes, with new demand for spices from Southeast Asia and textiles from India and China. Goods were now linked directly to the European market instead of passing through regional ports of the Indian Ocean.

In 1619 the Dutch, acting through the Dutch East India Company, took the city of Sunda Kelapa and renamed it Batavia, now Jakarta. They used it as a base for trading and for expansion into other parts of Java. In 1641 the Dutch also took Malacca from the Portuguese.
In 1599 Spain began to colonise the Philippines. It was one of the ways Spain, together with the Netherlands, came to supersede Portugal as a main European power in the region.

In 1592 Trịnh Tùng launched a massive invasion of the north and conquered Hanoi. The last significant Mạc ruler, Mạc Mậu Hợp, was captured during the retreat and cut to pieces over three days. The Mạc kept only Cao Bằng Province, under the formal protection of the Ming army.

The 17th-century war between the Trịnh and the Nguyễn ended in an uneasy peace, creating de facto separate states even though both professed loyalty to the same Lê dynasty. After 100 years of peace, the Nguyễn lords faced the Tây Sơn rebellion in 1774 and could not contain it.

The French missionary priest Pigneau de Behaine befriended Nguyễn Ánh, the most senior of the Nguyễn lords to escape the Tây Sơn rebellion in 1777. He became Nguyễn Ánh's confidant, benefactor and military advisor, and won great favor for the Church.

In 1775 the Lanfang Republic was established in West Kalimantan, possibly the first republic in the region. It was a tributary state of the Qing Empire. It lasted until 1884, when it fell under Dutch occupation as Qing influence waned.

The Kangxi Emperor demanded in 1667 that Trịnh Tạc return Cao Bằng Province to the Mạc after the Lê took it without Qing permission. In 1677 the Revolt of the Three Feudatories led the Qing to enlist Lê aid, and Mạc Kính Vũ was arrested as he fled into Guangxi. This ended the Mạc dynasty.

Yamada Nagamasa, leader of the Japanese settlement at Ayutthaya, opposed Prasat Thong's coronation. After King Prasat Thong changed trade regulations in 1629, Nagamasa was sent away as governor of Nakhon Si Thammarat, after strong opposition to his power from other Siamese officials. In 1630 he was assassinated, the settlement was burned, and its Japanese residents were killed by Siamese soldiers and Sheikh Ahmad, under the pretense of "rebellious activity". Many survivors fled into the nearby Khmer Empire.

The Nguyễn lords' military had suffered considerable losses in manpower after a series of campaigns in Cambodia. The Trịnh lords then formed an alliance with the Tây Sơn rebels and captured Huế in 1775.

In 1786 Captain Francis Light founded the settlement of George Town at the northeastern tip of Penang Island, under the administration of Sir John Macpherson. Britain had struggled with the French for naval superiority during its conflicts and needed good harbours, and Light had brought Penang to the attention of the Government of India. The settlement marked the beginning of British expansion into the Malay Peninsula.

philosophy.text: The most intense period of Islamization in Southeast Asia came between 1570 and 1630. During these years the region had direct commercial, religious and military contact with the Ottoman Caliphate and Mecca.

Catholicism first entered Vietnam through Portuguese and Spanish missionaries in the 16th century, though these early missions brought unimpressive results. Only after Jesuits arrived in the first decades of the 17th century did Christianity begin to establish itself in both Đàng Ngoài (Tonkin) and Đàng Trong (Cochinchina).

Islam spread outward in stages. By 1500 it had reached Selangor, Terengganu, North Sumatra and Northern East Java. By 1600 it covered the coastal Malay Peninsula, coastal Sumatra and North Java, and by 1700 it had reached the interior of Sumatra and Java and the coasts of Kalimantan and Sulawesi.

By the time Europeans and their missionaries arrived in the 17th century, the region was described as overwhelmed by Muslims, with animist minorities. Foreign accounts, however, sometimes told a different story.

The priests Francesco Buzomi and Diogo Carvalho established the first Catholic community in Hội An in 1615. The Jesuits who brought Christianity to Vietnam were mainly Italians, Portuguese and Japanese.

Tome Pires wrote in 1515 that three quarters of the population of the North Moluccas were still 'heathens'. In 1621 a Dutch resident reported no more than 300 Muslims in Ambon, showing how uneven the spread of Islam was.

Between 1627 and 1630, Avignonese Alexandre de Rhodes and the Portuguese Pero Marques converted more than 6,000 people in Tonkin. Their work helped Christianity gain a foothold among local populations.

After the 17th century, when Ming dynasty power declined, many Minh sects began to emerge in Cochinchina, especially around Saigon. Minh Đạo means the 'Way of Light' and belongs to the milieu of Chinese-Vietnamese religious sectarianism.

culture.text: Between 1570 and 1630, Islamization in Southeast Asia reached its most intense period. During these years there was direct commercial, religious and military contact with the Ottoman Caliphate and Mecca.
In Vietnam, Đạo Mẫu, the worship of mother goddesses, was established in the 16th century. It draws together various disparate beliefs and practices.

Anthony Reid's two-volume work covers the region from 1450 to 1680. It describes material culture, social organisation and leisure activity, and argues that the humid tropical environment, suited to rice agriculture and sea travel, explains similarities in material culture and even folk beliefs across the region.
culture.source_title: Southeast Asia in the Age of Commerce

culture.text: Islam in Southeast Asia often adapted to coexist with local traditions, and mysticism became a defining feature, with Sufism having a large regional following. Mystic forms of Islam fit in well with already established traditions. In Indonesia, the Abangan practise a form of Islam that incorporates rituals inherited from their pre-Islamic ancestors.

Reid's history was written from the perspective of the everyday life of the people. It earned him the Fukuoka Asian Culture Prize, largely on the strength of this book, and translations appeared in Indonesian, Japanese, Thai and Chinese.

culture.text: Arab merchants and cartographers called Maritime Southeast Asia Al-Jaza'ir Al-Jawi, or the Java archipelago. People from the region were commonly identified by the name 'Al-Jawi'.

When Europeans and missionaries arrived in the 17th century, the region was described as overwhelmed by Muslims. Yet foreign accounts told a different story: Tome Pires in 1515 said three quarters of the population of North Moluccas were still 'heathens', and in 1621 a Dutch resident reported no more than 300 Muslims in Ambon.
